slides.narration: A lift cable, a bridge girder and a rubber band all change shape when a load acts on them. Some return to their shape when the load is removed, and some do not. In this part we meet stress and strain, Hooke’s law, and the stress strain curve that tells an engineer how far a material can be trusted.

slides.heading: Elastic, plastic and elastomers
slides.body_md: A **deforming force** changes the size or shape of a solid; interatomic forces then try to restore it.
bullets: **Elasticity**: the property of regaining the original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.
**Plasticity**: the solid stays deformed. Putty and wet clay are close to perfectly plastic.
No real body is perfectly elastic; steel, quartz and phosphor bronze come close within limits.
Rubber is an **elastomer**: it returns even after huge strains, but its behaviour is not simply proportional.

rows: regains its original size and shape
steel spring, quartz fibre (within the limit)
putty, wet clay, a bent copper strip

rubber band, the wall of the aorta

visual.alt: Table comparing elastic, plastic and elastomeric behaviour with examples

slides.narration: When a force deforms a solid, the forces between its atoms pull it back. A body that regains its shape afterwards is called elastic, and one that stays deformed is called plastic. Steel and quartz are very nearly elastic inside their limits. Putty is plastic. Rubber is special: it returns to its shape even after a very large stretch, and it is called an elastomer.

slides.heading: Stress: restoring force per unit area
slides.body_md: In equilibrium the **restoring force** inside the body equals the applied force.
bullets: SI unit: pascal, Pa = N m⁻² (megapascal, MPa = 10⁶ Pa); dimensions M L⁻¹ T⁻².
Tensile (stretching) and compressive (squeezing) stress act perpendicular to the area: **longitudinal stress**.
**Shear stress**: force parallel to the face, per unit area of the face.
**Hydraulic stress**: the pressure p acting on every face.

slides.narration: Stress is the restoring force per unit area, force divided by area, measured in pascals. Pull on a rod and it is tensile, squeeze a pillar and it is compressive, and both act at right angles to the area. A force along the face gives shear stress. Pressure on all faces, like water on a submerged block, is hydraulic stress.

slides.heading: Strain: the fractional change
slides.body_md: Strain measures how much the body is deformed compared with its original size; it has **no unit**.
bullets: Longitudinal strain: change of length per original length.
Shear strain: the angle θ (in radian) through which the faces turn; for small angles tan θ ≈ θ.
Volume strain: change of volume per original volume.

slides.narration: Strain says how much a body has changed compared with its original size. Longitudinal strain is the extension divided by the original length. Shear strain is the sideways shift divided by the height, which is the angle of shear in radians. Volume strain is the change in volume divided by the original volume. Each is a ratio, so none of them has a unit.

slides.heading: Hooke’s law
slides.body_md: For small deformations the stress is directly proportional to the strain.
bullets: The constant is the **modulus of elasticity** of the material; it depends on the material and the kind of strain.
Within the limit, a graph of stress against strain is a straight line through the origin; its slope is the modulus.
For a spring the same idea reads F = k x: extension proportional to load.
Steel has the steepest line here: a given stress produces the smallest strain.

visual.alt: Stress against strain for steel, copper and aluminium within the elastic limit: three straight lines through the origin whose slopes are the Young moduli, steel the steepest
visual.caption: Within the limit, stress is proportional to strain; the slope is the modulus.

slides.narration: Hooke’s law says that for small deformations, stress is directly proportional to strain. The ratio is a constant called the modulus of elasticity, and it is the slope of the straight line on a stress strain graph. In the graph a steel wire gives the steepest line, so the same stress produces the least strain in steel.

slides.heading: The stress–strain curve of a ductile metal
slides.body_md: A wire is loaded slowly until it breaks; stress is plotted against strain.
bullets: **OA**: straight line, Hooke’s law holds. A is the **proportional limit**.
**B**: the **elastic limit** (here taken together with the **yield point**): beyond it the body does not fully recover.
**BC**: plastic region; the stress needed rises to the **ultimate stress** at C (the greatest stress the metal bears).
**CD**: the wire thins (necks) and **fractures** at D.

series.label: B: elastic limit and yield point (160 MPa)

visual.alt: Stress-strain curve of a ductile metal: a straight rise to the proportional limit A, a bend to the elastic limit and yield point B, a long plastic region rising to the ultimate stress C, then a fall to fracture at D
visual.caption: The metal behaves elastically up to B; between B and D the strain is largely permanent.

slides.narration: This is the stress strain curve of a ductile metal. Along the first straight part, Hooke’s law holds, and point A is the proportional limit. At B, the elastic limit and yield point, the metal stops recovering fully. Between B and C the strain is largely permanent. C is the ultimate stress, the highest stress the metal can bear, and the wire finally breaks at D.

slides.heading: Beyond the elastic limit: permanent set
slides.body_md: Stretch the wire to a point P beyond B, then remove the load slowly.
bullets: The stress falls along a line **parallel to OA**, not back along the loading curve.
At zero stress a **permanent strain** remains: $\varepsilon_\text{perm} = \varepsilon_P - \sigma_P / Y$.
Here P is at strain 0.012 and stress 231.4 MPa, so 0.00869 of strain is left.
A wire that has been stretched past its yield point stays longer: it has a permanent set.

series.label: unloading line, parallel to the first straight part
permanent strain 0.00869 left at zero stress

visual.alt: Stress-strain curve beyond the elastic limit with an unloading line drawn parallel to the first straight part: when the load is removed the stress falls to zero but a permanent strain of about 0.0087 remains
visual.caption: Unloading follows a line parallel to OA, so a permanent strain remains.

slides.narration: Suppose we stretch the wire to a point beyond the elastic limit and then slowly remove the load. The stress does not retrace the curve. It falls along a line parallel to the first straight part, and when the stress reaches zero a permanent strain of about 0.00869 is left. The wire is now permanently longer.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much load before yielding?
slides.body_md: A steel rod of cross-section $60$ mm$^2$ has a yield stress of $250$ MPa and an ultimate stress of $400$ MPa. Find the largest load that keeps it elastic, and the load at which it is about to break.
bullets: Yield load $= \sigma_y A = 250 \times 10^6 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-5} = 1.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N} = 15.0\ \text{kN}$.
Ultimate load $= \sigma_u A = 400 \times 10^6 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-5} = 2.40 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N} = 24.0\ \text{kN}$.
A designer keeps the working load well below the first value.

visual.alt: Table of the yield and ultimate stress of a steel rod, its area and the corresponding forces

slides.narration: Force is stress times area. The area is sixty square millimetres, which is six times ten to the minus five square metres. At the yield stress the load is 15.0 kilonewtons, the most the rod can carry and still recover. At the ultimate stress it is 24.0 kilonewtons, the load at which it is about to give way.

slides.heading: Ductile and brittle solids
slides.body_md: Materials differ in how far they stretch between the elastic limit and fracture.
bullets: **Ductile**: a long plastic region (copper, iron, aluminium). They can be drawn into wires and absorb a lot of energy before breaking.
**Brittle**: fracture soon after the elastic limit (glass, cast iron). They shatter with little warning.
The longer the plastic region, the more warning a structure gives before it fails.

visual.alt: A ductile metal curve with a long plastic region compared with a brittle solid, whose straight line stops at a small strain where it fractures
visual.caption: A brittle solid breaks soon after the elastic region; a ductile one stretches a long way first.

slides.narration: A ductile material, such as copper or iron, has a long plastic region, so it can be drawn into wire and gives warning before it fails. A brittle material, such as glass, breaks soon after the elastic limit, with very little stretch. On the graph the glass like line stops almost at once, while the metal curve continues.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the curve
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

series.label: B: elastic limit and yield point (160 MPa)

visual.alt: Stress-strain curve of a ductile metal: a straight rise to the proportional limit A, a bend to the elastic limit and yield point B, a long plastic region rising to the ultimate stress C, then a fall to fracture at D
visual.caption: The metal behaves elastically up to B; between B and D the strain is largely permanent.

slides.narration: Think about what the wire does after the load is removed once the yield point has been crossed.

slides.heading: Elastomers
slides.body_md: Rubber, and the wall of the aorta, can be stretched to several times their length and still recover.
bullets: The stress–strain curve is **not a straight line**: Hooke’s law fails, although the material is elastic.
There is **no well-defined plastic region**: the body keeps returning to its shape.
The strain is large for a small stress, so such a material is easy to stretch.

functions.label: straight line with the initial slope (Hooke)

visual.alt: Stress-strain curve of a rubber-like material up to a strain of five: it is curved, not a straight line, so Hooke law fails, and it keeps returning to its shape even after very large strain
visual.caption: An elastomer stretches many times its length yet is still elastic; its curve is not linear.

slides.narration: Rubber and the wall of the aorta are elastomers. They can be stretched to many times their original length and still spring back, but the curve is bent, not straight, so Hooke’s law does not hold. There is no clear plastic region. Notice that being elastic is not the same as being hard to stretch.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding where Hooke’s law ends
slides.body_md: In a school experiment a wire carries loads of $5, 10, \dots, 35$ N. The extensions are $0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60$ and $0.78$ mm. Up to which load does the wire obey Hooke’s law?
bullets: Extension per newton $= 0.10 / 5 = 0.02$ mm N$^{-1}$ for the first six readings.
Hooke prediction at 35 N: $0.02 \times 35 = 0.700$ mm.
Measured $0.78$ mm is larger by $0.080$ mm, so the limit is about $30$ N.

visual.alt: Load against extension for a wire in a school experiment: the first six points lie on a straight line through the origin, the seventh, at 35 newtons, lies above it
visual.caption: The first six readings obey Hooke; the last one has left the line.

slides.narration: For the first six readings every five newtons adds the same point one zero millimetres, so the ratio is steady. Hooke’s law would predict 0.700 millimetres at thirty five newtons, but we measured 0.78. The wire has left the straight line after thirty newtons, so that is about the limit of Hooke’s law.

slides.heading: Quick check: permanent set
slides.body_md: Work out the number.

series.label: unloading line, parallel to the first straight part
permanent strain 0.00869 left at zero stress

visual.alt: Stress-strain curve beyond the elastic limit with an unloading line drawn parallel to the first straight part: when the load is removed the stress falls to zero but a permanent strain of about 0.0087 remains
visual.caption: Unloading follows a line parallel to OA, so a permanent strain remains.

slides.narration: Use the unloading line, which is parallel to the first straight part of the curve.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: F / A in pascal; tensile, compressive, shear or hydraulic
ΔL / L, angle θ = Δx / h, or ΔV / V; no unit
stress ∝ strain within the proportional limit
A proportional limit, B elastic limit and yield point, C ultimate stress, D fracture
unloading is parallel to OA; a permanent strain remains
elastic but not linear; no clear plastic region

visual.alt: Summary table of stress, strain, Hooke’s law, the stress-strain curve and elastomers

slides.narration: To sum up. Stress is force per area and strain is the fractional change, a number with no unit. Hooke’s law says stress is proportional to strain within the proportional limit. On the curve, A is the proportional limit, B the elastic limit and yield point, C the ultimate stress and D the fracture. Beyond B, unloading leaves a permanent strain. Elastomers are elastic but not linear.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Convert diameter to radius and millimetre to metre before using A = πr²: the commonest slip.
Strain has no unit; if your strain carries one, you divided wrongly.
Name the points on the curve in order: proportional limit, elastic limit and yield point, ultimate stress, fracture.
Unloading beyond the elastic limit goes parallel to the initial line, not back along the loading curve.

rows: regains its original size and shape
steel spring, quartz fibre (within the limit)
putty, wet clay, a bent copper strip
regains its shape even after a very large strain, but not in proportion
rubber band, the wall of the aorta

visual.alt: Table comparing elastic, plastic and elastomeric behaviour with examples

slides.narration: Convert the diameter to a radius and millimetres to metres before using the area formula. Remember that strain has no unit. On the stress strain curve, name the points in order: proportional limit, elastic limit and yield point, ultimate stress and fracture. And when you unload beyond the elastic limit, draw the unloading line parallel to the first straight part.

slides.narration: Pull on three wires of equal size with the same load, one of steel, one of brass and one of aluminium. They stretch by different amounts. The number that describes this difference is the modulus of elasticity. In this part we meet three of them and use them for ropes, beams and the deep sea.

slides.heading: Young’s modulus
slides.body_md: For a wire of length L and area A stretched by ΔL under a force F:
bullets: SI unit: pascal (N m⁻²), the same as stress, since strain has no unit.
Y depends only on the **material**, not on the length or the thickness of the wire.
A larger Y means a stiffer material: less extension for the same stress.
The same value works for compression within the elastic limit.

headers: Extension of the 2.0 m, 1.0 mm wire at 200 N (mm)

visual.alt: Table of the Young moduli of steel, copper, brass and aluminium and the extension of an identical wire of each under 200 newtons

math: Y = \dfrac{\text{tensile stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} = \dfrac{F L}{A\,\Delta L}
slides.narration: Young’s modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to longitudinal strain. Written out, it is force times length divided by area times extension. Its unit is the pascal. It belongs to the material, not to the particular wire, so a thick wire and a thin one of the same metal have the same Young’s modulus. The table gives the values and the extension of one standard wire.

slides.heading: Same wire, same load, different metals
slides.body_md: Each wire is 2.0 m long and 1.0 mm in diameter, and carries 200 N.
bullets: Extension $\Delta L = \dfrac{F L}{A Y}$: inversely proportional to $Y$ for equal $F$, $L$ and $A$.
Steel stretches least; aluminium most.
In everyday speech we say steel is more elastic than rubber: it needs far more stress for the same strain.

Extension is inversely proportional to Young’s modulus, so the metal with the largest modulus stretches least. That is why steel is called more elastic than rubber: it takes far more stress to produce the same strain.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: Young’s modulus from an experiment
slides.body_md: A wire of length $2$ m and diameter $0.8$ mm extends by $2$ mm under a load of $100$ N. Find its Young modulus.
bullets: $Y = \dfrac{1.99 \times 10^{8}}{0.001} = 1.99 \times 10^{11}$ Pa: the wire is steel.

visual.alt: Table of the steps to find the Young modulus of a wire from a measured load and extension

slides.narration: First find the area, about 5.03 times ten to the minus 7 square metres, then the stress, 1.99 times ten to the 8 pascals. The strain is two millimetres divided by two thousand millimetres, which is point zero zero one. Dividing, Young’s modulus comes to 1.99 times ten to the 11 pascals, which matches steel.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: stretch of a lift cable
slides.body_md: A steel cable of length $30$ m and cross-section $4.0$ cm$^2$ supports a load of mass $1500$ kg ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$, $Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11}$ Pa). Find its extension.
bullets: $\Delta L = \text{strain} \times L = 1.84 \times 10^{-4} \times 30 = 5.51 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 5.51\ \text{mm}$.

visual.alt: Extension against load for a 2.0 metre wire of diameter 1.0 millimetre in steel, brass and aluminium: three straight lines, the steepest for aluminium, which has the smallest Young modulus
visual.caption: Slope = L / (A Y): the smaller the modulus, the steeper the line.

slides.narration: The weight is 14700 newtons. Divided by the area, the stress is 3.67 times ten to the 7 pascals. Dividing by Young’s modulus gives a strain of 1.84 times ten to the minus 4. Multiplying by thirty metres, the cable stretches by only 5.51 millimetres, which shows how stiff steel is.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

visual.caption: Slope = L / (A Y): the smaller the modulus, the steeper the line.

slides.narration: Use the fact that, for equal force, length and area, the extension is inversely proportional to the Young modulus.

slides.heading: Shear modulus
slides.body_md: A tangential force F on a face of area A turns the faces through the angle θ.
bullets: Also called the **modulus of rigidity**; SI unit pascal.
Only solids have a shear modulus: a fluid cannot resist a sideways force, it flows.
For most metals G is smaller than Y, roughly Y / 3.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: shear of a steel plate
slides.body_md: A force of $42$ kN acts along the top face of a steel block, $0.2$ m by $0.25$ m, of height $0.1$ m. For steel $G = 8.4 \times 10^{10}$ Pa. Find the shear angle and the sideways shift of the top face.
bullets: $\theta = \text{stress}/G = \dfrac{8.4 \times 10^{5}}{8.4 \times 10^{10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ rad.
$\Delta x = \theta h = 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.1 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m, about one micrometre.

slides.narration: Squeeze a body equally from all sides and its volume falls. The bulk modulus is the pressure increase divided by the fractional decrease in volume, with a minus sign so that it comes out positive. Its reciprocal is the compressibility. Unlike the other moduli, it applies to liquids and gases as well as solids.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: water at the bottom of the sea
slides.body_md: At a depth of $4$ km the extra pressure of sea water is $\rho g h$, with $\rho = 1000$ kg m$^{-3}$ and $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$. By what fraction does the volume of water shrink? ($B = 2.2 \times 10^9$ Pa)
bullets: $p = \rho g h = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 4000 = 3.92 \times 10^{7}$ Pa.
$\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{p}{B} = \dfrac{3.92 \times 10^{7}}{2.2 \times 10^{9}} = 0.0178$, about 1.78 percent.
So each $1$ m$^3$ of water loses about $17.8$ litres.

visual.alt: Fractional decrease of the volume of sea water against the increase of pressure: a straight line, about 1.8 percent at 4 kilometres depth and 4.5 percent at 10 kilometres

slides.narration: The extra pressure at four kilometres depth is density times g times depth, 3.92 times ten to the 7 pascals. Dividing by the bulk modulus of water gives a fractional decrease of 0.0178, about 1.78 percent. A cubic metre of water would lose roughly 17.8 litres. Even at this depth water is only slightly compressed.

slides.heading: The three moduli side by side
slides.body_md: Each modulus is a stress divided by the matching strain.
bullets: Same unit for all three: pascal.
A bigger modulus means a stiffer response; a gas has a tiny bulk modulus and a solid a huge one.
A material can be stiff in one way and soft in another: rubber shears and stretches easily but resists compression strongly.

rows: tangential force per area, F / A

slides.narration: Here are the three moduli together. Young’s modulus links tensile stress to longitudinal strain. The shear modulus links shear stress to the angle of shear. The bulk modulus links pressure to volume strain. All three have the unit pascal, and a bigger modulus means a stiffer material for that kind of deformation.

slides.heading: Cranes, lifts and ropes
slides.body_md: Elastic behaviour decides how a rope is designed.
bullets: The rope’s breaking stress is a property of the steel; the rope must never be loaded near it.
**Safety factor** = breaking stress ÷ working stress, often 8 to 10 for lifting ropes.
The cross-section is chosen so that the working stress is well inside the elastic region.
A rope of many thin strands is flexible; a solid rod of the same area would be too stiff to bend over a pulley.

rows: flexible over a pulley, yet the total cross-section carries the load
Working stress = breaking stress ÷ safety factor
keeps the rope far below its elastic limit even with jerks and ageing
Check the stretch ΔL = F L / (A Y)
a long rope under load must not extend too much

visual.alt: Table of design choices for crane and lift ropes and the reason for each

slides.narration: A crane or lift rope must never be loaded near its breaking stress. Engineers divide the breaking stress by a safety factor, often eight to ten, to get the working stress, and then choose the cross section so the load gives only that stress. The rope is made of many thin strands so that it stays flexible over pulleys.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: choosing lift ropes
slides.body_md: A lift of total mass $2500$ kg hangs from $4$ identical steel ropes. Steel of breaking stress $4.0 \times 10^8$ Pa is used with a safety factor of $8$. Find the least radius of each rope (treat each as solid; $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$).
bullets: Load on one rope $= 2500 \times 9.8 / 4 = 6125$ N.
Working stress $= 4.0 \times 10^8 / 8 = 5.0 \times 10^{7}$ Pa.
$A = F / \text{stress} = 1.22 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^2$, so $r = \sqrt{A/\pi} = 6.24$ mm.

visual.alt: Table of the steps to find the radius of each lift rope using a safety factor

slides.narration: Each rope carries a quarter of the weight, 6125 newtons. With a safety factor of eight the working stress is 5.0 times ten to the 7 pascals. The area is the load divided by that stress, 1.22 times ten to the minus 4 square metres, and the radius from the area comes to 6.24 millimetres.

slides.heading: Beams, girders and bridges
slides.body_md: A beam on two supports with a load sags: the top layers are compressed and the bottom layers are stretched.
bullets: A middle layer keeps its length; material near it carries little stress.
The largest stresses are at the top and bottom surfaces, so beams are made **I-shaped**: wide flanges far from the middle, a thin web between.
For the same material and load, a **deeper** beam sags much less than a shallow one; a stiffer material (larger Y) also sags less.
This saves material and weight in bridges and building frames.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: comparing two wires
slides.body_md: Wire B has twice the length and twice the radius of wire A; both are of the same material and carry the same load. Compare their extensions.
bullets: $\Delta L = \dfrac{F L}{A Y} = \dfrac{F L}{\pi r^2 Y} \propto \dfrac{L}{r^2}$ for the same $F$ and $Y$.
$\dfrac{\Delta L_B}{\Delta L_A} = \dfrac{2}{2^2} = 0.50$.
A longer wire stretches more; a thicker wire stretches less, with the square of the radius.

visual.alt: Table comparing the extension of two wires of the same material under the same load with different lengths and radii

slides.narration: Extension is proportional to length divided by the square of the radius. Wire B has twice the length, which doubles the extension, and twice the radius, which cuts it to a quarter. The ratio is two divided by four, which is 0.50. So the longer, thicker wire stretches half as much as wire A.

Steel: $\Delta L = F L / (A Y) = 1.146$ mm; copper: $1.389$ mm.

notes.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Stress, strain and Hooke’s law
sections.body_md:
- A **deforming force** changes the size or shape of a solid; a body that regains its original size and shape when the force is removed is **elastic**, one that stays deformed is **plastic**. No real body is perfectly elastic.
- **Stress** is the restoring force per unit area, $F/A$, in pascal (Pa = N m$^{-2}$; dimensions $\text{M L}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}$). Longitudinal stress is **tensile** (stretching) or **compressive** (squeezing); **shear stress** acts along a face; **hydraulic stress** is the pressure on all faces.
- **Strain** is the fractional change and has no unit: longitudinal strain $\Delta L/L$, shear strain $\Delta x/h = \tan\theta \approx \theta$, volume strain $\Delta V/V$.
- **Hooke's law:** for small deformations stress is proportional to strain; the ratio is the **modulus of elasticity**. Example: a steel wire of diameter 1.6 mm, length 2.5 m, carrying 150 N and stretching 0.8 mm has stress $7.46 \times 10^{7}$ Pa and strain $3.2 \times 10^{-4}$.
- **Stress–strain curve of a ductile metal:** A proportional limit (Hooke's law ends), B elastic limit and yield point (beyond it the body does not fully recover), C ultimate stress (the greatest stress), D fracture. Beyond B, unloading follows a line parallel to OA and leaves a **permanent strain** (here 0.00869 after stretching to strain 0.012).
- **Ductile** materials (copper, iron) have a long plastic region; **brittle** ones (glass, cast iron) fracture soon after the elastic limit. **Elastomers** (rubber, the aorta) stretch to several times their length and recover, but the curve is not a straight line and there is no clear plastic region.
- In a school experiment, loads of 5 N steps give $0.02$ mm N$^{-1}$ up to 30 N; at 35 N the extension (0.78 mm) exceeds the Hooke value (0.700 mm), so the wire has left the proportional range. A rod of 60 mm$^2$ with yield stress 250 MPa carries 15.0 kN without yielding.

sections.heading: 2. Elastic moduli and applications of elastic behaviour
sections.body_md:
- **Young's modulus** $Y = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$: it belongs to the material, not to the wire. For equal $F$, $L$ and $A$ the extension is inversely proportional to $Y$: steel ($2.0 \times 10^{11}$ Pa) stretches less than copper ($1.1 \times 10^{11}$), brass ($9.1 \times 10^{10}$) or aluminium ($7.0 \times 10^{10}$). Steel is called more elastic than rubber because it needs a much greater stress for the same strain.
- **Shear modulus (modulus of rigidity)** $G = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta}$; only solids have it. For many metals $G$ is about $Y/3$. A steel plate ($G = 8.4 \times 10^{10}$ Pa) under 42 kN on a face of 0.05 m$^2$ shears by $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ rad, a shift of $1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m over 0.1 m.
- **Bulk modulus** $B = -\dfrac{p}{\Delta V/V}$; compressibility $k = 1/B$. Solids, liquids and gases all have $B$. At 4 km depth the pressure rise of sea water is $\rho g h = 3.92 \times 10^{7}$ Pa, so with $B = 2.2 \times 10^9$ Pa its volume falls by 1.78 percent.
- **Wire extension:** $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{\pi r^2 Y}$ — proportional to $L/r^2$ and inversely to $Y$. Doubling both length and radius halves the extension (factor 0.50). Two wires joined end to end carry the same force and their extensions add: a steel wire of 1.5 m and a copper wire of 1 m (1.0 mm diameter) under 120 N stretch 2.535 mm in all. A steel cable of 30 m and 4.0 cm$^2$ under 1500 kg ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$) stretches 5.51 mm; the wire in worked example 4 gives $Y = 1.99 \times 10^{11}$ Pa.
- **Ropes and cranes:** working stress = breaking stress ÷ safety factor. Lift ropes of total 2500 kg on 4 ropes with a safety factor 8 and breaking stress $4.0 \times 10^8$ Pa need a radius of 6.24 mm each. A rope made of many thin strands is flexible but still has the full cross-section.
- **Beams and bridges:** a loaded beam is compressed above and stretched below, with a middle layer unchanged. Because the stress is largest at the top and bottom, girders are I-shaped, and a deeper beam of the same material sags far less than a shallow one.
- Left out here: Poisson's ratio and the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire; they are not named in the syllabus topics and were cut from the rationalised book.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Convert diameter to radius and millimetre to metre before A = πr²; strain has no unit.
- Name the points on the stress–strain curve in order; unloading beyond the elastic limit is parallel to the first straight part.
- Say which modulus applies; liquids and gases have only a bulk modulus.
- Wires joined end to end: same force, extensions add. Same wire stretched: ΔL = FL/(AY).
- For ropes and cranes use working stress = breaking stress ÷ safety factor.

cards.front_md: What does an elastic body do when the deforming force is removed?
cards.back_md: It regains its original size and shape (within its elastic limit).

cards.front_md: Which is closer to perfectly plastic: putty or quartz fibre?
cards.back_md: Putty.

cards.front_md: Define stress and give its SI unit.
cards.back_md: Restoring force per unit area, F/A; pascal (N m⁻²).

cards.front_md: Name the four kinds of stress.
cards.back_md: Tensile, compressive, shear and hydraulic.

cards.front_md: Why does strain have no unit?
cards.back_md: It is a ratio of two like quantities (lengths or volumes).

cards.front_md: Write the shear strain for a top face displaced by Δx on a block of height h.
cards.back_md: Δx/h = tan θ ≈ θ (radian).

cards.front_md: State Hooke’s law.
cards.back_md: Within the proportional limit, stress is proportional to strain.

cards.front_md: What does the slope of the straight part of a stress–strain graph give?
cards.back_md: The modulus of elasticity (Young’s modulus for a stretched wire).

cards.front_md: What is the elastic limit?
cards.back_md: The greatest stress up to which the body returns to its original shape when unloaded.

cards.front_md: What is the ultimate stress?
cards.back_md: The greatest stress the material can bear on the curve, just before fracture.

cards.front_md: A wire is stretched past its yield point and unloaded. How does the stress fall?
cards.back_md: Along a line parallel to the first straight part, leaving a permanent strain.

cards.front_md: Give one ductile and one brittle material.
cards.back_md: Ductile: copper (or iron); brittle: glass (or cast iron).

cards.front_md: What is an elastomer? Give two examples.
cards.back_md: A material elastic to very large strain but not obeying Hooke’s law: rubber, the aorta wall.

cards.front_md: A rod of 60 mm² cross-section yields at 250 MPa. Load at yield?
cards.back_md: 15 kN (stress × area).

cards.front_md: Write Young’s modulus in terms of F, A, L and ΔL.
cards.back_md: Y = FL/(AΔL).

cards.front_md: On what does Young’s modulus of a wire depend?
cards.back_md: Only on the material, not on length or thickness.

cards.front_md: Which has the larger Young modulus: steel or aluminium?
cards.back_md: Steel (2.0 × 10¹¹ against 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa).

cards.front_md: Equal wires of steel and copper carry the same load. Which stretches less?
cards.back_md: Steel, since its Young modulus is larger.

cards.front_md: Why is steel said to be more elastic than rubber?
cards.back_md: It needs a much larger stress for the same strain (larger modulus).

cards.front_md: Define the shear modulus.
cards.back_md: Shear stress divided by shear strain: G = F/(Aθ).

cards.front_md: Why does a liquid have no shear modulus?
cards.back_md: It cannot resist a sideways force: it flows.

cards.front_md: Define the bulk modulus.
cards.back_md: B = −p/(ΔV/V): pressure increase over fractional volume decrease.

cards.front_md: What is compressibility?
cards.back_md: The reciprocal of the bulk modulus, 1/B.

cards.front_md: Which moduli can a gas have?
cards.back_md: Only the bulk modulus.

cards.front_md: Two wires of the same material and load: A has length L and radius r, B has 2L and 2r. Ratio of extensions B : A?
cards.back_md: 1 : 2, since extension ∝ L/r².

cards.front_md: Wires joined end to end carry a load. What is common to both and what adds?
cards.back_md: The force is the same; the extensions add.

cards.front_md: Define the safety factor of a rope.
cards.back_md: Breaking stress divided by the working stress.

cards.front_md: Why is a crane rope made of many thin strands?
cards.back_md: It stays flexible over pulleys while the total cross-section carries the load.

cards.front_md: Why is a girder I-shaped?
cards.back_md: Stress from bending is largest at the top and bottom, so material is placed there; it saves weight.

cards.front_md: In a bent beam, which layers are compressed and which are stretched?
cards.back_md: The upper layers are compressed and the lower layers stretched when it sags under a load.

questions.stem_md: A civil engineer reports that the stress in a suspension-bridge cable is 180 MPa. Which statement about stress and its unit is correct?

options.text_md: Stress is force per unit length; its SI unit is N m⁻¹
Stress is a dimensionless ratio, so "MPa" is only a label
Stress is force multiplied by area; its SI unit is N m²
Stress is force per unit area; 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻², so 180 MPa = 1.8 × 10⁸ Pa

questions.solution_md: Stress is the restoring force per unit area, F/A, with unit N m⁻² = Pa; "mega" means 10⁶, so 180 MPa = 1.8 × 10⁸ Pa — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nylon rope 2.0 m long stretches by 1.0 mm when a cyclist ties her bag to it. The longitudinal strain in the rope is

options.text_md: 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, with no unit
2.0 × 10³, with no unit

questions.solution_md: Strain = ΔL/L = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m / 2.0 m = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴; a ratio of two lengths has no unit — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two steel wires, P and Q, each of cross-section 2.0 mm², hang from a ceiling and carry the same load. P is 1.0 m long and Q is 3.0 m long. Within the elastic limit, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The stresses are equal, and Q stretches three times as much as P
The stress in Q is three times that in P, and the extensions are equal
The stresses are equal, and the extensions are equal
The stress in Q is one-third of that in P, and Q stretches three times as much

questions.solution_md: Stress = F/A depends on the load and the area only, so it is the same in both. Strain is the same too (same stress, same material), so the extension ΔL = strain × L is three times larger for the three-times-longer wire — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student loads a copper wire in steps until it breaks and plots stress against strain. Hooke’s law applies to the part of the graph that is

options.text_md: the whole curve from the origin up to fracture
the initial straight line through the origin, up to the proportional limit
only the region beyond the yield point, where the wire flows
only the single point of ultimate stress

questions.solution_md: Hooke’s law (stress ∝ strain) holds only along the initial straight part, up to the proportional limit; beyond it the curve bends — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A steel wire is stretched until its stress is well past the yield point and then the load is removed slowly. Which statement describes the wire afterwards?

options.text_md: It returns to exactly its original length
It becomes shorter than its original length
It is longer than its original length: a permanent strain remains
It breaks the moment the load is removed

questions.solution_md: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is plastic; unloading follows a line parallel to the initial straight part and reaches zero stress at a non-zero strain, so the wire stays longer — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A hardware workshop draws copper into thin wire but cannot do the same with glass rods. This is because copper is

options.text_md: brittle, with a long plastic region
perfectly elastic, with no plastic region at all
an elastomer that obeys Hooke’s law right up to fracture
ductile, with a long plastic region between its elastic limit and fracture

questions.solution_md: A ductile metal can be stretched permanently by a large amount before it breaks, so it can be drawn into wire; glass is brittle and fractures soon after its elastic limit — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A rubber band is stretched to four times its original length and springs back when released. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Rubber obeys Hooke’s law up to this strain, because it recovers completely
Rubber is plastic, because it stretches by a large amount
Rubber has a larger Young modulus than steel, because it stretches more
Rubber is an elastomer: elastic up to a very large strain, but its stress–strain curve is not a straight line

questions.solution_md: An elastomer recovers after very large strains, but stress is not proportional to strain and there is no clear plastic region. Easy stretching means a small modulus, not a large one — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A metal wire stretched well beyond its elastic limit stays longer than before when the load is removed.

**Reason (R):** Beyond the elastic limit the wire has undergone plastic deformation, so a permanent strain is left.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true and R explains A: plastic deformation does not reverse on unloading — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A strain of 0.0005 in a copper wire is measured in pascal, the same unit as stress.

**Reason (R):** Strain is the ratio of the change in length to the original length, so it has no unit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: strain is a pure number with no unit. R is true. So the correct option is (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A rubber band returns to its original length after being stretched to three times that length, so it must obey Hooke’s law over the whole stretch.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Rubber is elastic over a very large strain, but its stress–strain curve is not a straight line, so stress is not proportional to strain over this range. Being elastic is not the same as obeying Hooke’s law.

questions.stem_md: On the stress–strain curve of a drawn copper wire, the greatest stress reached before the wire necks and breaks is called the ___ stress.
questions.solution_md: It is the **ultimate** stress (the highest point of the curve), after which the wire thins and fractures.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor’s steel tape 30 m long stretches by 3 mm when pulled tight. The ratio 3 mm / 30 m is its ___ strain.
questions.solution_md: The change of length divided by the original length is the **longitudinal** strain.

questions.stem_md: Each row of Column A describes a stress on a body. Match it with the strain it produces in Column B.

options.text_md: Tensile stress on a hanging cable
Shear stress on a block pushed sideways along its top face
Water pressure on all faces of a submerged steel cube
Compressive stress on a short brick pillar

match_right.text_md: Angle through which the faces turn

questions.solution_md: Tensile stress: ΔL/L increase. Shear stress: the angle of shear θ = Δx/h. Hydraulic stress: −ΔV/V. Compressive stress: ΔL/L decrease.

questions.stem_md: A steel wire of diameter 1.2 mm supports a load of 60 N. Find the stress in the wire, in MPa (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.60 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 1.13 \times 10^{-6}$ m$^2$. Stress $= \dfrac{F}{A} \approx \dfrac{60}{1.13 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 5.31 \times 10^{7}$ Pa $= 53.1$ MPa.

questions.stem_md: A 1.5 m long rope used to tie a tent stretches by 0.90 mm under the pull of the wind. Find the longitudinal strain, in units of 10⁻⁴.
questions.solution_md: Strain $= \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{0.90 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5} = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}$. In units of $10^{-4}$: strain $= 6$.

marking_scheme.step: Strain = ΔL/L with both lengths in metres

questions.stem_md: A pull rod made of an aluminium alloy has a cross-section of 35 mm² and a yield stress of 160 MPa. Find the largest load, in kN, that the rod can carry without exceeding its yield stress.

marking_scheme.step: F = yield stress × area = 5600 N = 5.6 kN

questions.stem_md: A steel wire in a laboratory extends by 0.45 mm under a load of 30 N. Assuming Hooke’s law holds, find its extension under a load of 80 N, in mm.
questions.solution_md: Extension is proportional to load: $e_2 = e_1 \times \dfrac{F_2}{F_1} = 0.45 \times \dfrac{80}{30} = 1.2$ mm.

questions.stem_md: A steel specimen with Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa is stretched beyond its elastic limit to a strain of 4.0 × 10⁻³, where the stress is 3.0 × 10⁸ Pa. The load is then removed slowly along a line parallel to the initial straight part of the curve. Find the permanent strain left, in units of 10⁻³.
questions.solution_md: Strain recovered $= \dfrac{\sigma}{Y} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.0 \times 10^{11}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$. Permanent strain $= 4.0 \times 10^{-3} - 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$. In units of $10^{-3}$: permanent strain $= 2.5$.

marking_scheme.step: Unloading line is parallel to OA: recovered strain = σ/Y = 1.5 × 10⁻³

questions.stem_md: A copper wire of diameter 1.0 mm breaks when the stress in it reaches its ultimate stress, 3.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the largest mass that can be hung from it before it breaks, in kg (2 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $A = \pi (0.50 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 7.85 \times 10^{-7}$ m$^2$. Breaking force $F = \sigma_u A \approx 235.6$ N. Mass $= \dfrac{F}{g} \approx \dfrac{235.6}{9.8} = 24$ kg.

questions.stem_md: Two metal plates are joined by a glue layer of area 25 cm². The glue fails when the shear stress in it reaches 8.0 × 10⁶ Pa. Find the largest force, acting along the layer, that the joint can carry, in kN.
questions.solution_md: $A = 25 \times 10^{-4}$ m$^2$. Shear stress $= F/A$, so $F = 8.0 \times 10^{6} \times 25 \times 10^{-4} = 20000\ \text{N} = 20$ kN.

marking_scheme.step: F = shear stress × area = 20000 N = 20 kN

questions.stem_md: The top face of a rubber block of height 8.0 cm is pushed sideways by 0.20 mm relative to its fixed base. Find the shear strain (the angle of shear), in units of 10⁻³ rad.
questions.solution_md: $\theta \approx \tan\theta = \dfrac{\Delta x}{h} = \dfrac{0.20 \times 10^{-3}}{8.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ rad. In units of $10^{-3}$ rad: $\theta = 2.5$.

marking_scheme.step: θ ≈ Δx/h with both lengths in metres

questions.stem_md: A steel spring in a kitchen scale and a lump of putty are each pulled and then released. Use them to distinguish elastic from plastic behaviour.

answer.model_answer_md: The steel spring is **elastic**: when the pulling force is removed it regains its original shape, because the interatomic forces restore it. The putty is **plastic**: it stays deformed after the force is removed. No real body is perfectly elastic or perfectly plastic.

questions.solution_md: Spring regains shape; putty does not.

marking_scheme.step: Elastic body regains original size and shape (spring)

questions.stem_md: A technician stretches a wire and finds that doubling the load doubles its extension. State Hooke’s law and say what she can conclude about the stress and the strain in the wire.

answer.model_answer_md: **Hooke’s law:** within the proportional limit, stress is directly proportional to strain. Doubling the load doubles the stress (same area) and the extension doubles the strain (same length), so the ratio of stress to strain is constant and the wire is still within the Hooke range.

questions.solution_md: Stress ∝ strain; both double.

marking_scheme.step: Statement: stress ∝ strain within the limit
Both stress and strain double; ratio constant

questions.stem_md: On the stress–strain curve of a ductile metal, explain what is meant by (i) the yield point and (ii) the ultimate stress.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **yield point** (with the elastic limit) is the stress beyond which the metal no longer recovers fully; permanent, plastic strain begins. (ii) The **ultimate stress** is the greatest stress on the curve, the highest the material can bear before it thins and fractures.

questions.solution_md: Yield: start of permanent strain. Ultimate: greatest stress.

marking_scheme.step: Yield point: beyond it deformation is permanent (plastic)
Ultimate stress: the maximum stress on the curve

questions.stem_md: A hanging cable and a block pushed sideways along its top face show different kinds of stress. Name the stress and the matching strain for each.

answer.model_answer_md: For the hanging cable the stress is **tensile (longitudinal) stress**, F/A, and the strain is **longitudinal strain**, ΔL/L. For the block pushed along its face the stress is **shear stress**, F/A with F parallel to the face, and the strain is the **angle of shear** θ ≈ Δx/h.

questions.solution_md: Tensile: ΔL/L. Shear: θ = Δx/h.

marking_scheme.step: Block: shear stress and the angle of shear Δx/h

questions.stem_md: Describe the stress–strain curve of a ductile metal wire, naming the points from the proportional limit to fracture.

answer.model_answer_md: The curve starts as a straight line, OA, where stress is proportional to strain; A is the **proportional limit**. Up to B, the **elastic limit and yield point**, the wire still recovers. Beyond B the strain is largely permanent (plastic region) and the stress needed rises to the **ultimate stress** at C. After C the wire thins and **fractures** at D.

questions.solution_md: OA straight; A, B, C, D named.

marking_scheme.step: OA straight line, A proportional limit
B elastic limit and yield point; plastic region beyond
C ultimate stress; fracture at D

questions.stem_md: A wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and the load is then removed slowly. Describe, with the shape of the unloading graph, what happens to the wire and why.

answer.model_answer_md: On the stress–strain graph the unloading path is a straight line **parallel to the initial straight part**, not the loading curve. It reaches zero stress at a **non-zero strain**, the permanent set, so the wire stays longer. Beyond the elastic limit the layers of atoms have slipped to new positions (plastic deformation), so the original shape is not recovered.

questions.solution_md: Parallel to OA; permanent strain remains.

marking_scheme.step: Unloading line is parallel to the first straight part
Zero stress at non-zero strain: permanent set
Reason: plastic deformation beyond the elastic limit

questions.stem_md: A steel girder and a glass plate each fail under tension. Compare ductile and brittle behaviour using the stress–strain curve, and say why ductile materials are preferred for bridges.

answer.model_answer_md: A **ductile** material such as steel has a long plastic region between the elastic limit and fracture: it stretches and sags visibly before failing. A **brittle** material such as glass fractures soon after its elastic limit, with little strain and no warning. Bridges use ductile steel because a long plastic region gives warning and absorbs energy before collapse.

questions.solution_md: Long vs short plastic region; warning.

marking_scheme.step: Brittle: fracture soon after the elastic limit

questions.stem_md: A copper wire is cut into two pieces, one twice as long as the other, and the shorter piece is then hammered thinner. The Young modulus of the two pieces compares as

options.text_md: the longer piece has twice the value
equal, because it depends only on the material
the thinner piece has the larger value
the shorter piece has twice the value

questions.solution_md: Young’s modulus Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) is a property of the material; length and thickness cancel out of the ratio — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two wires of identical length and diameter, one of steel (Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa) and one of copper (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), carry the same load within their elastic limits. The ratio (extension of steel) : (extension of copper) is

options.text_md: 1.8: the steel wire stretches more
0.55: the steel wire stretches less
1.00: both stretch equally because they have equal size
0.30: the steel wire stretches less

questions.solution_md: For equal F, L and A the extension ΔL = FL/(AY) is inversely proportional to Y: ΔL_steel/ΔL_Cu = Y_Cu/Y_steel = (1.1 × 10¹¹)/(2.0 × 10¹¹) = 0.55 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A sealed syringe is full of water, and pushing the plunger compresses the water very slightly. Of Young’s modulus, the shear modulus and the bulk modulus, the water has

options.text_md: all three moduli, just like steel
a Young modulus and a shear modulus but no bulk modulus
only a bulk modulus: it resists change of volume but flows under a sideways force and has no fixed shape
a shear modulus only, because it is under pressure

questions.solution_md: A fluid cannot sustain a shear stress (it flows), so it has no shear modulus; it is the volume that changes under pressure, so the bulk modulus applies — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A rubber pad lies between a bridge girder and its pier. A horizontal force parallel to the top face makes the top face slide a little. The elastic constant that describes this deformation is the

options.text_md: shear modulus (modulus of rigidity): tangential stress divided by the angle of shear
Young modulus: tensile stress divided by longitudinal strain
bulk modulus: pressure change divided by fractional change of volume
compressibility: fractional change of volume per unit pressure

questions.solution_md: A force along the face is a shear stress and the strain is the angle of shear, so the relevant modulus is G = (F/A)/θ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The bulk moduli of three substances are: air 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, water 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa and steel 1.6 × 10¹¹ Pa. Which is the most compressible, and what is its compressibility?

options.text_md: steel, 6.3 × 10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹
air, 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ Pa⁻¹
water, 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹
air, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa⁻¹

questions.solution_md: Compressibility = 1/B. The smallest modulus gives the largest compressibility: air, 1/(1.0 × 10⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ Pa⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A wire P of radius r carries a load F and stretches by e. A second wire Q of the same material and length has radius 2r and carries a load 2F. Within the elastic limit the extension of Q is

options.text_md: 2e
e

questions.solution_md: ΔL = FL/(πr²Y) ∝ F/r². For Q: (2F)/(2r)² = F/(2r²), which is one half of P’s F/r², so the extension is e/2 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The steel rope of a port crane is made of many thin wires twisted together rather than of one solid steel rod of the same total cross-section. The main reason is that the rope

options.text_md: has a lower breaking stress, so it needs a smaller safety factor
has a larger Young modulus than a solid rod of the same steel
bends easily over a pulley while the combined cross-section still carries the load
does not stretch at all, so no safety factor is needed

questions.solution_md: Many thin strands are flexible, yet the sum of their cross-sections carries the load. Young’s modulus is a property of the steel, and a safety factor is needed for any rope — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Steel girders in a railway bridge have an I-shaped cross-section, with most of the steel in the top and bottom flanges. This is because

options.text_md: steel is stronger in the shape of the letter I than in any other shape
the middle layer carries the greatest stress, so it must be thin to save weight
the top and bottom layers do not stretch or compress at all
the stress from bending is greatest at the top and bottom layers, so material there resists bending best for the weight used

questions.solution_md: In a bent beam the top layers are compressed and the bottom layers stretched, the middle layer is unchanged; the largest stresses are far from the middle, so material is placed there — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Sea water has bulk modulus 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa. At a depth where the pressure is higher than at the surface by 4.4 × 10⁷ Pa, the fractional decrease in the volume of the water is

**Assertion (A):** Steel is considered more elastic than rubber.

**Reason (R):** Rubber can be stretched to a much larger strain than steel before it fractures.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: A steel cable 40 m long, of cross-section 3.0 cm², lifts a load of mass 1200 kg at a construction site. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻² and Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa, find the extension of the cable, in mm.

questions.stem_md: A sealed steel sphere of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is lowered into an ocean trench where the pressure is 8.0 × 10⁷ Pa higher than at the surface. The bulk modulus of steel is 1.6 × 10¹¹ Pa. Find the decrease in volume of the sphere, in cm³.

The extra pressure at that depth is ρgh, with ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.8 m s⁻²; the bulk modulus of water is 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa. Find the decrease in the volume of the water, in cm³ (1 litre = 1000 cm³).

questions.stem_md: Two wires of the same material and the same length carry the same load. Wire 1 has radius 0.50 mm and wire 2 has radius 1.5 mm. Find the ratio (extension of wire 1) : (extension of wire 2).
questions.solution_md: $\Delta L = \dfrac{F L}{\pi r^2 Y} \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for equal $F$, $L$ and $Y$. So $\dfrac{\Delta L_1}{\Delta L_2} = \left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1.5}{0.50}\right)^2 = 9$.

questions.stem_md: An aluminium wire 1.2 m long is joined end to end to a steel wire 0.80 m long; both have diameter 0.80 mm. The combination carries a load of 90 N. Taking Y = 7.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa for aluminium and 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa for steel, find the total extension, in mm.

questions.stem_md: Define Young’s modulus and state its SI unit. Why do a thick copper wire and a thin copper wire have the same value of it?

answer.model_answer_md: **Young’s modulus** is the ratio of tensile stress to longitudinal strain, Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL); its unit is the pascal. Stress is force per area and strain is extension per length, so size cancels out: the value depends only on the **material**, hence thick and thin copper wires share it.

questions.solution_md: Stress/strain; pascal; material property.

marking_scheme.step: Definition Y = stress/strain with unit pascal
Depends only on the material (size cancels)

questions.stem_md: Why can a liquid have a bulk modulus but no shear modulus?

answer.model_answer_md: A **bulk modulus** needs only a change of volume under pressure, and a liquid resists that. A **shear modulus** needs the body to resist a sideways force with a fixed shape, but a liquid **flows** under any shear stress, so it cannot maintain a shear strain.

questions.solution_md: Volume resisted; flows under shear.

marking_scheme.step: Liquid resists change of volume: bulk modulus exists
Liquid flows under shear stress: no shear modulus

questions.stem_md: A designer must carry the same bending load on a bridge with the least weight of steel. Explain why she chooses an I-shaped girder instead of a solid square bar.

answer.model_answer_md: When a girder bends, the **top layers are compressed**, the bottom layers are stretched and the middle layer is unchanged, so stress is largest at the top and bottom. An **I-section** puts most of the steel in those flanges and little in the lightly stressed middle, so the girder is as stiff as a solid bar of much greater weight.

questions.solution_md: Stress greatest at top and bottom; material placed there.

marking_scheme.step: Bending stress greatest far from the middle layer
I-section puts material in flanges: same stiffness for less steel

questions.stem_md: A student says: "Rubber stretches far more than steel, so rubber is more elastic." Explain whether she is right, using Young’s modulus.

answer.model_answer_md: She is **wrong**. Elasticity is about regaining shape and about how large a stress is needed for a given strain, measured by the modulus. For the same stress steel gives a very small strain, so its Young modulus (about 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa) is much larger than that of rubber. Rubber stretches easily, but it needs a far smaller stress per unit strain, so it has the smaller modulus.

questions.solution_md: Larger Y means more elastic; steel has the larger Y.

marking_scheme.step: Elasticity judged by stress needed per unit strain (modulus)
Steel: small strain for a given stress, large Y
Rubber stretches easily because Y is small; so steel is more elastic

questions.stem_md: A crane lifts heavy steel girders with a rope made of many thin twisted wires. Explain why a safety factor is used and why the rope has many thin strands.

answer.model_answer_md: The **safety factor** is the breaking stress divided by the working stress. Using a rope of enough cross-section so that the working stress is a small fraction (say one-tenth) of the breaking stress keeps it inside the elastic region even with jerks and ageing. **Many thin strands** make the rope flexible over pulleys, while the total cross-section still carries the load.

questions.solution_md: Safety factor; flexibility.

marking_scheme.step: Safety factor = breaking stress ÷ working stress
Keeps the rope in the elastic region despite jerks and ageing
Many strands: flexible, same total cross-section

questions.stem_md: Name the three elastic moduli of a material. For each, state the kind of stress, the kind of strain, and one body to which it applies.

answer.model_answer_md: **Young’s modulus** = tensile or compressive stress ÷ longitudinal strain (ΔL/L); a stretched steel wire. **Shear modulus** = shear stress ÷ angle of shear θ; a rubber pad under a sideways force (solids only). **Bulk modulus** = pressure change ÷ fractional change of volume (−ΔV/V); water in a sealed vessel (solids, liquids or gases).

questions.solution_md: Y, G and B with stress, strain and example.

marking_scheme.step: Young: tensile stress ÷ ΔL/L, stretched wire
Shear: shear stress ÷ θ, rubber pad (solids)

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe the stress–strain curve of a ductile metal wire, naming the proportional limit, the elastic limit and yield point, the ultimate stress and the fracture point, and saying how the wire behaves in each region. (b) A wire of diameter 1.4 mm has a yield stress of 3.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Find the largest load it can carry without a permanent change of length.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The curve starts as a straight line OA: stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law), and A is the **proportional limit**. Up to B, the **elastic limit and yield point**, the wire still returns to its original length on unloading. Beyond B the deformation is largely **plastic**: the stress rises to the **ultimate stress** at C, the greatest on the curve, and then the wire thins and **fractures** at D. A ductile metal has a long BD.

(b) $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.70 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 1.54 \times 10^{-6}$ m$^2$. The load stays elastic while the stress does not exceed the yield stress, so $F = \sigma_y A \approx 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 1.54 \times 10^{-6} \approx 461.8$ N.

questions.solution_md: Regions OA, B, C, D; area 1.54 × 10⁻⁶ m²; F about 462 N.

marking_scheme.step: Straight line OA, Hooke’s law; A proportional limit; B elastic limit/yield point
Plastic region BC to the ultimate stress; thinning and fracture at D
Behaviour in each region described (recovers up to B, permanent beyond)

questions.stem_md: (a) Define Young’s modulus and write the formula for it in terms of F, A, L and ΔL. (b) A steel wire 3.0 m long and 1.0 mm in diameter carries a load of mass 5.0 kg (g = 9.8 m s⁻², Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa for steel). Find the stress, the strain and the extension. (c) The steel wire is replaced by a copper wire of the same size (Y = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa), assumed to stay within its elastic limit. Find the new extension and compare it with the first.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Young's modulus** is the ratio of tensile stress to longitudinal strain: $Y = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} = \dfrac{F L}{A\,\Delta L}$.

(b) $F = mg = 5.0 \times 9.8 = 49$ N; $A = \pi (0.50 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 7.85 \times 10^{-7}$ m$^2$. Stress $= \dfrac{F}{A} \approx 6.24 \times 10^{7}$ Pa. Strain $= \dfrac{\text{stress}}{Y} \approx \dfrac{6.24 \times 10^{7}}{2.0 \times 10^{11}} \approx 3.12 \times 10^{-4}$. Extension $\Delta L = \text{strain} \times L \approx 9.36 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m} = 0.936$ mm.

(c) For copper, $\Delta L \propto 1/Y$: $\Delta L_{Cu} = 0.936 \times \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{11}}{1.1 \times 10^{11}} \approx 1.70$ mm, about 1.8 times the steel value, because the Young modulus of copper is smaller.

questions.solution_md: Definition; stress 6.24e7 Pa, strain 3.12e-4, extension 0.936 mm; copper 1.70 mm.

marking_scheme.step: Compared: 1.8 times larger, since Y is smaller

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the shear modulus and the bulk modulus. (b) A force of 5.0 × 10⁴ N acts along one face of an aluminium cube of side 0.10 m whose opposite face is fixed. Taking the shear modulus of aluminium as 2.5 × 10¹⁰ Pa, find the angle of shear and the displacement of the loaded face. (c) A copper sphere of volume 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³ is subjected to an extra all-round pressure of 7.0 × 10⁷ Pa. For copper B = 1.4 × 10¹¹ Pa; find the decrease in its volume.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **shear modulus** is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain, $G = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta}$, where $\theta = \Delta x/h$ is the angle of shear. The **bulk modulus** is the ratio of the pressure increase to the fractional decrease of volume, $B = -\dfrac{p}{\Delta V/V}$.

(b) Face area $= 0.10^2 = 0.01$ m$^2$; shear stress $= \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{4}}{0.01} = 5.0 \times 10^{6}$ Pa. $\theta = \dfrac{\tau}{G} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{6}}{2.5 \times 10^{10}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ rad. Displacement $\Delta x = \theta h = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.10 = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m} = 0.020$ mm.

(c) $|\Delta V| = \dfrac{p V}{B} = \dfrac{7.0 \times 10^{7} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{1.4 \times 10^{11}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^3 = 0.20$ cm³.

questions.solution_md: G and B defined; θ = 2.0e-4 rad, Δx = 0.020 mm; ΔV = 0.20 cm³.

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by the safety factor of a rope, and why is a crane rope made of many thin strands? (b) A port crane lifts a container of mass 12 tonnes with two identical steel ropes sharing the load equally. The steel has breaking stress 6.0 × 10⁸ Pa and a safety factor of 6 is used; take g = 9.8 m s⁻² and treat each rope as solid. Find the least radius of each rope. questions.stem_md: (a) A steel wire is joined end to end to a brass wire and the combination carries a load. State which quantity is the same in the two wires and which quantities add. Find the extension of each wire and the total extension. (c) Which wire has the larger strain, and why?
